cases.title: Obi Island nickel mines and smelters: Kawasi's water and fishing grounds
cases.place: Kawasi village, Obi Island, South Halmahera, North Maluku, Indonesia
cases.point: Kawasi village on Obi Island (OpenStreetMap village point), next to the Harita Group mines and the Halmahera Persada Lygend smelter

lenders.name: DBS, BNP Paribas, Bank Mandiri, BCA, BNI, Maybank, OCBC, OCBC NISP and UOB
lenders.role: A consortium of nine banks, jointly led by Singapore's DBS, launched a US$625 million project financing for PT Halmahera Persada Lygend's high pressure acid leach (HPAL) nickel smelter, announced on 1 April 2021 (DBS).

lenders.name: Lygend (China)
lenders.role: China's Lygend Mining co-owns the roughly US$1 billion site with Indonesia's Harita Group (The Guardian).

cases.conditions: Project finance for Indonesia's first HPAL smelter, which makes nickel products for electric-car batteries; DBS acted as a lead coordinator, mandated lead arranger and facility agent (DBS, 2021).

companies.name: Lygend Resources & Technology
companies.role: Chinese co-owner of PT Halmahera Persada Lygend with the Harita Group (The Guardian)

companies.name: Harita Group
companies.role: Indonesian owner of the Obi nickel mines (PT Trimegah Bangun Persada, PT Gane Permai Sentosa) and co-owner of the smelter

cases.community: Water from a fountain used for household water near Kawasi, less than 200 metres from the mining site, tested at 60 parts per billion of hexavalent chromium (Cr6) in samples the Guardian took to government-certified laboratories; Indonesia's legal limit is 50 ppb (The Guardian, 2022). The village midwife clinic recorded more than 900 cases of acute respiratory infection among about 4,000 residents in 2020, more than half in children aged four and under; health officials put prevalence at just under 20%, against a national average of 9% (The Guardian). Fishers say it now takes at least three days at sea to catch 10 kg of tuna, and that the sea turns red in the rainy season (Mongabay).
cases.ecosystem: An unpublished 2019 Khairun University study found heavy metals linked to nickel mining above normal levels off the island's southern coast and in at least 12 marine species, including clams and mangrove snappers (Mongabay). In 2019 authorities approved PT Trimegah Bangun Persada's plan to dump 6 million tonnes of waste a year into the sea; the company dropped it after protests and then sought to clear forest for a tailings dam (Mongabay).
cases.outcome: The company says its own tests of Kawasi's spring from 2013 to 2021 found 5 to 40 ppb of Cr6, within government standards, and that the project was approved through a government environmental assessment (The Guardian). Mining and smelting continue.

sources.title: 'We are afraid': Erin Brockovich pollutant linked to global electric car boom
Red seas and no fish: Nickel mining takes its toll on Indonesia's spice islands
DBS launches USD 625 million financing structure for PT Halmahera Persada Lygend
Nickel rush threatens the health and environment of Obi Island's people, Indonesia

cases.confidence_note: The Cr6 result comes from water samples the Guardian commissioned; the company's own monitoring reported lower values within the legal limit and it says it does not discharge Cr6. Nickel mining on Obi began in 2007-2008 and the 2020 respiratory-infection figures predate the 2021 bank loan; the date the Chinese co-owner joined is not given in the cited sources. The Cr6 sampling (2022) came after the loan. The link between the respiratory infections and the mines is the view of local health workers, not a medical study.

lvwhy.project: Foreign-owned and bank-financed smelting expanded a nickel complex beside a fishing village.
lvwhy.finance: Nine banks arranged US$625 million in project finance for the HPAL smelter in 2021 (DBS).

cases.title: Tilenga oilfield and EACOP pipeline: land taken from Ugandan farmers
cases.place: Buliisa, Hoima and other districts along the EACOP route, Uganda
cases.point: Buliisa district, site of the Tilenga oilfield where the pipeline starts (approximate; the land acquisition covers five districts)

lenders.name: TotalEnergies (France)
lenders.role: Majority shareholder of EACOP Ltd and operator of both the pipeline and the Tilenga oilfields through TotalEnergies EP Uganda; Reuters reports a 62% stake in the pipeline (HRW; Business Day/Reuters).

lenders.name: China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC)
lenders.role: Chinese state-owned partner in the Tilenga oilfields and shareholder of EACOP Ltd (HRW).

cases.conditions: TotalEnergies' subsidiaries ran land acquisition for the pipeline corridor and the Tilenga oilfield; by 2023 TotalEnergies said compensation had been paid to 93% of affected pipeline households (HRW).

companies.name: TotalEnergies
companies.role: Operator of Tilenga and EACOP, majority shareholder in EACOP Ltd

companies.name: CNOOC
companies.role: Chinese state-owned partner in Tilenga and EACOP

cases.community: Human Rights Watch interviewed 75 displaced families in five Ugandan districts in early 2023 and found most were worse off: compensation came three to five years after valuation, was too low to buy replacement land, and families were pressed to take cash instead of land (HRW). During the delays farmers understood they could not tend perennial crops; families sold livestock, borrowed at high rates, and took children out of school (HRW). HRW calculates that over 100,000 people in Uganda and Tanzania will permanently lose land to the pipeline and Tilenga (HRW).
cases.suppression: Families who refused to sign described pressure from company officials, threats of court action and harassment by local government and security officials; in Tilenga, land of those who held out for replacement land was expropriated through the courts, with compensation deposited in court (HRW).
cases.outcome: TotalEnergies says compensation met full replacement value and added a 15% per year uplift for delays and a livelihood programme of at least three years (HRW). Preliminary ground work on the pipeline began in 2023 (Business Day/Reuters). The later arrests of students protesting bank funding of EACOP are on a separate card.

sources.title: 'Our Trust is Broken': Loss of Land and Livelihoods for Oil Development in Uganda
Human Rights Watch says Uganda pipeline is disaster for people and planet
East Africa Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), Uganda and Tanzania

cases.confidence_note: TotalEnergies rejects the findings; its spokesperson told Reuters nearly all affected people had been compensated and were being relocated to better living conditions. The 100,000 figure is HRW's calculation from project documents of people who will permanently lose land, not a count of people already displaced. HRW's findings rest on interviews with 75 displaced families.

lvwhy.land: Company-run land acquisition paid late cash compensation that families say could not replace their land (HRW).
lvwhy.project: Foreign oil companies own and operate the oilfield and pipeline that required the land.

cases.title: Pacitan coal plant: fishers' catches and coal dust
cases.place: Sumberejo and Sukorejo villages, Sudimoro, Pacitan, East Java, Indonesia
cases.point: Pacitan power station, Sudimoro (Global Energy Monitor coordinates)

lenders.name: Export-Import Bank of China
lenders.role: Lent US$293.23 million to the state utility PLN, agreed in July 2009, to finance the 2 x 315 MW Pacitan coal plant; 12-year tenor with two years' grace (Petromindo; Global Energy Monitor).

cases.conditions: Loan to PLN for a 630 MW coal plant built under Indonesia's 2006 crash programme of 10,000 MW of new plants (Global Energy Monitor; Mongabay).
cases.community: Fishers from Sumberejo stopped fishing in Kondang Bay after construction began in 2007; one former fishers' group leader said his high-season shrimp catch fell from up to 12 million rupiah (US$902) a day to about 200,000 rupiah (US$15), and that the plant paid a one-time 26 million rupiah to the group (Mongabay). Villagers report coal dust in homes in the dry season, a polluted river, beach erosion at Ndaki, cracked house walls and a road damaged by overloaded vehicles; after an October 2016 meeting the plant sent masks, soap and mops (Mongabay).
cases.ecosystem: Village leaders say the river near the plant is polluted and no longer has young fish, and that the plant's structures focused the waves on Ndaki Beach, causing erosion (Mongabay).
cases.outcome: The plant has operated since 2013; the company says its operations have not affected water quality (Mongabay). In 2023 the energy ministry listed it as a possible target for early retirement (Global Energy Monitor).

sources.title: Pacitan villagers say coal plant reduced livelihoods, brought little new employment
In response to pollution complaints, a coal plant in Indonesia offered soap and mops
PLN secures $293 million of loan from Cexim
Pacitan power station
Coal fired power plant near conservation areas in Pacitan, East Java, Indonesia

cases.confidence_note: The harm rests on residents' and village leaders' accounts reported by Mongabay; no official measurement of dust or fish stocks was found, and the company says its operations have not affected water quality. Construction began in 2007, before the July 2009 China Exim loan (the plant was 72% built at signing, per Petromindo); the fishing losses and dust complaints continued after the plant started in 2013. Dongfang Electric is named as builder only by EJAtlas and is listed as a contractor, not as the outside link.

lvwhy.project: A Chinese state bank loan financed the coal plant built in a fishing bay.

cases.title: Tanjung Kasam coal plant: coal dust on Batam homes
cases.place: Telaga Punggur and Teluk Nipah, Nongsa, Batam, Riau Islands, Indonesia
cases.point: PLTU Tanjung Kasam at Telaga Punggur, Kabil, Nongsa, Batam (OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: Export-Import Bank of China and Sinosure
lenders.role: China Eximbank gave a seller's credit to China Huadian Engineering, which used it to fund a US$150 million supplier credit to the plant's owner, PT Tanjung Kasam Power, signed on 21 November 2008; the borrower bought credit insurance from Sinosure (AidData).

cases.conditions: Supplier credit of US$150 million (10-year maturity, 3-year grace) to part-finance the US$181 million construction contract for a 130 MW coal plant; construction began in March 2011 and the plant started at the end of 2012 (AidData).

companies.name: China Huadian Engineering Co.
companies.role: Chinese construction contractor that passed on the China Eximbank credit to the owner (AidData)

cases.community: Residents of Telaga Punggur have complained of breathing and skin problems from the plant's ash since it started at the end of 2012, and about 300 residents rallied to shut it (The Jakarta Post, February 2013). Residents of Telaga Punggur and Teluk Nipah said dust from unloading coal thickened on walls and roofs and some people had respiratory illness; a neighbourhood head said the nearby clinic was mostly treating breathing problems caused by coal dust (Kompas, February 2013). A 22-year-old resident brought an X-ray from Elisabeth Hospital showing a lung infection and TB to a meeting with plant managers; a neighbour said the doctor blamed the dust, and the managers promised to pay for her treatment (Tribun Batam).
cases.suppression: Police stopped residents as they approached the plant's managers on 2 January 2013 to demand that it be shut down (The Jakarta Post; AidData).
cases.outcome: PLN Batam refused to stop the plant, which supplied about 26% of Batam's electricity, and said it was spraying coal before unloading to reduce dust (Kompas). The plant kept operating.

sources.title: Tanjung Kasam 130MW Coal-Fired Power Plant (Batam, Indonesia), project 62206
PLTU Diprotes Warga
Residents protest ash from Batam power plant
Katrina Ikut Demo di PLTU Tanjung Kasam Tunjukkan Hasil Rontgen
Tanjung Kasam Coal-fired Power Plant, Indonesia

cases.confidence_note: The health effects are residents' accounts and one doctor's reported view, as told to the press; no official air-quality measurement was found. PLN Batam said it was wetting the coal before unloading to reduce dust and could not stop the plant. The Jakarta Post gives the plant as 2 x 55 MW and 30% of Batam's demand; AidData gives 130 MW and Kompas 26%.

lvwhy.project: A China Eximbank-funded credit paid for building the coal plant next to two neighbourhoods.

cases.title: N-Sukala sugar estate: village land cleared in the Office du Niger
cases.place: M'Bewani zone, Office du Niger, Ségou region, Mali
cases.point: N'Sukala settlement, Cercle de Niono, in the Office du Niger area where the estate cleared land (OpenStreetMap; approximate for the cleared zone)

lenders.name: China Light Industrial Corporation for Foreign Economic and Technical Cooperation (CLETC)
lenders.role: Chinese state company that holds a 50-year renewable lease on about 20,000 ha (857 ha with title) under a 2009 agreement with Mali, which holds 40% of N-Sukala (Oakland Institute; Djiré et al., IIED/FAO).

cases.conditions: The 2009 agreement leased 19,143 ha for 50 years at an annual rent of 382,747,500 CFA francs (about US$772,778) and ceded 857 ha with title for 1.5 billion CFA francs; Mali's rent goes toward buying its 40% share (Oakland Institute). Article 7 of the contract makes the Chinese side responsible for the cost of informing, moving and resettling villages (Djiré et al.). The contracts give the Sukala and SOSUMAR sugar estates 'absolute priority' over Office du Niger water in proportion to their cane area if drought cuts the river's flow (Djiré et al.).

companies.name: CLETC (Sinolight group)
companies.role: Majority owner of N-Sukala SA and of the older Sukala SA sugar company (60%)

cases.community: In the M'Bewani area, N-Sukala began clearing land that belonged to local villages and was used for grazing, firewood and dry-season cereal crops, without a prior environmental and social impact study or adequate public consultation; local people received no prior compensation (Djiré et al., IIED/FAO, 2012).
cases.ecosystem: Village land used for grazing and firewood collection was cleared for cane without a prior environmental and social impact study (Djiré et al., IIED/FAO).
cases.outcome: The sugar estate and refinery were built and are in operation; EJAtlas reports that protests and sit-ins continue.

sources.title: Current dynamics of large-scale agricultural investments and inclusive business models in Mali: trends and case studies (M. Djiré, A. Kéita, A. Diawara)
Understanding Land Investment Deals in Africa: Mali
NSukala Sugar plantation and refinery in Cercle de Segou, Mali

cases.confidence_note: The number of people who lost land to N-Sukala is not given in the IIED/FAO or Oakland Institute reports; EJAtlas lists at least 8 villages (31,470 people). The sources describe clearing without prior compensation but do not say whether compensation was later paid. The water-priority clause is a contract term, not a recorded shortage.

lvwhy.land: Mali leased about 20,000 ha of village farmland and grazing land to a Chinese state company for 50 years.
lvwhy.project: The sugar estate was cleared before an impact study or compensation (Djiré et al.).

cases.title: Chirano gold mine: Sefwi cocoa farmers underpaid for their land
cases.place: Chirano area, Bibiani-Anhwiaso-Bekwai district, Western North Region, Ghana
cases.point: Chirano village, in the Chirano gold mine's operating area (OpenStreetMap village point)

lenders.name: Red Back Mining and Kinross Gold (Canada)
lenders.role: Canadian Red Back Mining obtained the mining lease in April 2004 and began production in October 2005; Kinross Gold bought Red Back in 2010 and owns the mine (MiningWatch Canada).

cases.conditions: A mining lease granted in 2004; Ghana's mining law requires prompt, fair and adequate compensation for disturbed surface rights (EJAtlas).

companies.name: Kinross Gold
companies.role: Owner of Chirano Gold Mines since 2010 (90%, with the Government of Ghana holding 10%, per EJAtlas)

companies.name: Red Back Mining
companies.role: Original Canadian owner that took the land in 2004-2006

cases.community: Between 2004 and 2006 the company paid some farmers 2.5 cedis per mature cocoa tree, telling them the government rate was 2.3 cedis; the official rate approved by the Land Valuation Board in 2003 was 5.22 cedis (MiningWatch Canada; Daily Post Ghana). Farmers went to court in 2006 and again in 2007; on 16 May 2012 the Minister of Lands directed the Land Valuation Division to secure payment of its recommended compensation, and the Division told the company to pay, but in October 2012 farmers in mourning cloth said it was still unpaid and threatened to reoccupy their land (MiningWatch Canada; Daily Post Ghana).
cases.outcome: EJAtlas reports that in early 2015 farmers who had accepted the low rate were paid the difference with some interest, while others were still waiting. Kinross says payments made from 2003 to 2005 were higher than standard crop valuation methods and were accepted by the farmers (MiningWatch Canada, quoting Kinross's 2011 report).

sources.title: Ghanaian Farmers Run Out of Patience with Kinross/Chirano Gold Mines
Sefwi farmers threaten to take over Chirano Gold Mines lands
Ghana: Forum calls for major mining reforms
Chirano Gold Mines compensation struggle, Ghana

cases.confidence_note: The number of farmers affected is not given in the cited sources. Kinross maintains the compensation was fair and accepted; the 2015 partial settlement is reported only by EJAtlas.

lvwhy.land: A Canadian-owned mine took cocoa farms and paid less than half the official crop rate (MiningWatch Canada).

cases.title: Busanga dam: village homes destroyed for the Sicomines power plant
cases.place: Kamalenge, Monga Lubuza, Wafinya and nearby villages, Busanga, Lualaba province, DR Congo
cases.point: Busanga dam on the Lualaba River, Lubudi territory (OpenStreetMap dam point); the cleared villages lie around the reservoir

lenders.name: Sinohydro and China Railway Group (Sicohydro joint venture)
lenders.role: Chinese state-owned companies in the Sicohydro joint venture with Gécamines that is building the US$660 million, 240 MW dam under the Sino-Congolese Sicomines minerals-for-infrastructure deal; the plant is to supply 170 MW to the Sicomines copper-cobalt mine (Green Building Africa; Afrewatch et al.).

cases.conditions: The dam is part of the 2007 Sicomines agreement, in which Chinese companies build infrastructure in exchange for copper and cobalt mining rights (Green Building Africa). Civil society groups say the Congolese side holds only 25% of the dam company, split between the private firm COMAN (15%), Gécamines (7%) and the power utility SNEL (3%) (Afrewatch et al.).
cases.community: In July 2020 the provincial interior minister ordered residents who had already received compensation to leave by 29 July so Sicohydro could dig the reservoir basin; eleven civil society groups warned that at least four villages were threatened and asked for more time (Green Building Africa; Actualite.cd). Demolition of houses at the village of '48 Heure' began in early October 2020 (Actualite.cd, 4 October 2020). A statement by 53 Congolese organisations, including Caritas Kolwezi and ASADHO, said that on 3 October 2020 three villages ('48 Heure', Monga Lubuza and Kamalenge) with more than 1,000 buildings were destroyed on the governor's instruction and with Sicohydro, while legal challenges were pending, leaving residents sleeping in the open on nearby mining concessions and at Kyamasumba village (Actualite.cd, 8 October 2020). In May 2021 civil society groups said Sicohydro had forcibly evicted farmers at Monga Lubuzo, Wafinia, Kibese and Disanga and destroyed about 900 homes since October 2020 without fair compensation (Afrewatch et al.). In September 2021 the Mwangaza network said displaced communities' fields were flooded with no compensation (Actualite.cd).
cases.suppression: The 53 organisations said provincial authorities sent police and the army to oversee the 3 October 2020 demolitions; earlier, nine groups had protested the use of security forces to clear residents (Actualite.cd).
cases.outcome: Construction continued. Civil society groups asked President Tshisekedi to halt the demolitions (October 2020) and to order an inquiry into the project (May 2021), and in September 2021 called on the national and provincial governments to organise compensation (Actualite.cd; Afrewatch et al.).

Projet Busanga: le gouvernement appelé à s'impliquer pour l'indemnisation des communautés locales

sources.title: Busanga Dam on Lualaba River, DRC

Which Chinese bank, if any, lent for the dam is not stated in the sources; the link is through the Chinese state companies that co-own and build it.

lvwhy.land: Villages were cleared for the reservoir; groups say more than 1,000 buildings were destroyed in October 2020 (Actualite.cd).

cases.title: Gwadar port and Eastbay Expressway: fishers pushed off the bay
cases.place: East bay and Mulla Band, Gwadar, Balochistan, Pakistan
cases.point: Gwadar's east bay, where the port and the Eastbay Expressway meet the fishing grounds (approximate)

lenders.name: China Ministry of Commerce (interest-free loan)
lenders.role: Interest-free loan of RMB 1.1 billion (about US$140 million; 20-year maturity, 10-year grace) for the Gwadar Eastbay Expressway, signed in 2017; construction by China Communications Construction Co. began on 22 November 2017 and the road opened in June 2022 (AidData).

lenders.name: Government of China and China Overseas Ports Holding Company
lenders.role: China provided 80% of the US$248 million initial development cost of Gwadar port, inaugurated in 2007; the port's expansion is being built under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (Arab News).

cases.conditions: The Eastbay Expressway is a CPEC project: a six-lane road with a 30-metre rail corridor linking the port to the Makran Coastal Highway through the port's 2,300-acre free trade zone (Dawn), financed by the Chinese interest-free loan (AidData).

companies.name: China Communications Construction Co. (CCCC)
companies.role: Chinese state-owned contractor that built the expressway (AidData)

cases.community: Arab News reported in 2019, without naming a source, that port expansion had displaced around 800 fishermen who lived on or near the port, the first displacement having come when port construction began in 2007; a fisherman at Dimi Zarr said expressway construction on the east bay, where most fishing takes place, had disrupted their work (Arab News). In December 2018 fishermen protested for 12 days, saying the expressway had cut off their routes to the Arabian Sea; they struck on 27 and 28 December, and on 27 December the daily shipment of fresh fish to Dubai, Riyadh and Kuwait could not leave because the market had no fish (Dawn).
cases.outcome: The government said it would allow three passages for boats under the expressway; the maritime affairs minister said the Gwadar Development Authority had accepted the fishermen's design demands and that their concerns had been addressed (Arab News). The expressway opened in June 2022 (AidData).

sources.title: Fishermen hope, and worry, as China builds giant port in Pakistan's Gwadar
Gwadar fishermen protest against construction of CPEC's project enters 12th day
Chinese Government provides RMB 1.1 billion interest-free loan for Gwadar Eastbay Expressway Construction Project

cases.confidence_note: The figure of about 800 displaced fishermen is given by Arab News without a named source and no count from the port or government was found. The harm to fishing rests on fishermen's statements reported by Dawn and Arab News; no catch or income figures were found. The government says the redesign settled the fishermen's concerns.

lvwhy.project: A Chinese-funded port and expressway took over the shore and bay used by fishers.
lvwhy.finance: A Chinese government interest-free loan of RMB 1.1 billion paid for the Eastbay Expressway (AidData).

dropped.candidate: Azura-Edo gas power plant: two villages resettled
dropped.reason: No actual harm confirmed. The household counts (34 and 12 homes, etc.) are MIGA's 2012 summary of the planned resettlement 'under its current design'. OPIC's later information summary (dfc.gov) says land was acquired from the Ihovbor community, who did not need to be resettled because nearly all lived in Benin City, and that all affected Ihovbor people were fully compensated in May 2014, witnessed by the independent consultant. The ERA claim of 20% compensation rests on EJAtlas only. A 2024 Edo State item on 1,962 people being paid for the Azura transmission-line right of way records payment, not harm.

dropped.candidate: Bishoftu (Abusera) mega airport: farmers moved off their land
dropped.reason: Timing/link not met yet. Displacement has happened: Ethiopian Airlines says 2,500 farmers were displaced and re-housed in 2025 and that rehabilitation was largely complete by mid-2026 (Arab News/AFP; Capital Ethiopia, Aug 2026). But AfDB's only signed role is the 11 August 2025 mandate as lead arranger to raise debt; its US$500 million loan is 'earmarked... subject to Board approval' (AfDB via AFP/Oman Observer, Aug 2025) and was still awaiting board approval/appraisal in August 2026, with lender approvals expected by March 2027 (Capital Ethiopia; Travel Extra). No outside money has been committed, so the resettlement cannot yet be tied to AfDB lending. Revisit if AfDB's board approves the loan.

dropped.candidate: Addu City land reclamation: coral and seagrass buried under new land
dropped.reason: No confirmed actual damage from the India Exim-financed Van Oord reclamation. The coral (21 ha), seagrass and US$17.4-27.4m tourism figures are the project EIA's pre-works estimates (HRW). Fishers' testimony to HRW concerns the earlier Feydhoo reclamation. The one reported die-off (April 2023, Maradhoo/Hankede) was blamed by #SaveMaldives on Van Oord but attributed by Atoll Times (23 April 2023) to reclamation for a bridge built by Afcons, a separate road project; Edition.mv reports Van Oord's physical works began in May 2023, after the die-off.

dropped.candidate: Noor Ouarzazate solar complex: collective land sold to the state solar agency
dropped.reason: No actual harm documented. The World Bank records a voluntary 'willing-buyer, willing-seller' purchase of ~3,000 ha of collective land it describes as arid, unoccupied and of little economic value, with no physical resettlement; the MAD 30.5 million price went to community projects (wells, irrigation, drinking water). The critic's study (Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung) objects to the process and low price but documents no lost grazing, income, water or homes. Process complaints alone do not pass the harm test.
